Scores between the siting rubric (which allows for desktop analysis) and onsite engineering inspection varied by an increase of 8% to a decrease of 13%, with the average change of 6%, indicating effectiveness of the rubric for narrowing potential sites prior to investing in engineering. The observed conditions that were most likely to cause a shift of project scoring (e.g. concrete cracks on reservoirs, roof condition, etc.) are potentially observable by city staff and may indicate an opportunity for further staff revision of potential projects prior to engagement of outside consulting firms. Final rubric scores for projects are found above (Figure 6). Evaluations included assessment of blue sky and resilience benefits for adding battery storage. Potential benefits included peak shifting and demand charge reduction, focused on sites with existing loads. Valuation of other benefits during a grid outage, for example reduction of delivered fuel usage for generators, generator wear, or potential of economic impacts of pumping stations being offline, were not included in the analysis. The City of Duluth has generator solutions for water treatment and pumping, and emergency government facilities (firehalls/police stations), reducing the potential resilience return for battery storage added to these facilities. Two sites were evaluated to have significant demand charges that could be reduced through battery installation. Research • Community-based Minimum Resilience Standards approved by 90% Methodologies or greater of Critical Infrastructure and Leadership Team F3 made it a priority to get input from City departments, community partners, and individual residents to create a holistic picture of what is needed for resilience. This research and engagement began with focus groups generating feedback from the community and project partners to guide solar infrastructure planning. By using an all- inclusive research method that is rarely deployed by municipalities, the project was able to capture resident experiences with a focus on vulnerable populations to enhance the understanding of community energy and resilience needs that could be addressed by community PV and storage implementation. The City of Duluth’s project partner, community-based organization Ecolibrium3, led the community-based research element for F3. Ecolibrium3 trained community volunteers to lead a tabletop exercise and host focus groups that concentrated on understanding lived-experiences of participants. Needs of vulnerable populations in disadvantaged communities were identified though oversampling in neighborhoods identified through the Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool as being disadvantaged. Information from the tabletop and focus groups were then incorporated into a research plan that was vetted by the Community Stakeholder Group, representing diverse community organizations.
